candidates.attacker_control: Any party able to influence a single configuration value (a property/value in a properties, XML, INI, plist, YAML or JSON file; a JNDI/JDBC/servlet/applet attribute; or a value passed to setProperty/addProperty from external input, e.g. tenant or user settings). Interpolation is performed when the application reads the value with a converting getter, not at load time, so the payload can arrive from remote or persisted data and detonate on later read.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the dangerous prefixes are restricted, filtered or opt-in: ConfigurationInterpolator's map is built once from DefaultLookups + Commons Text DefaultStringLookup with no allow-list, and AbstractConfiguration.installDefaultInterpolator() registers all of them on every construction (lines 128-135, 452-456). Checked whether interpolation only occurs on explicit request: DefaultConversionHandler.to() and extractConversionValue() interpolate on any typed conversion, so ordinary getString/getInt calls are sufficient; only getProperty() is raw. Checked whether a deployment can disable it: setPrefixLookups/deregisterLookup exist but are not applied by default and the 2.7 userguide (src/site/xdoc/userguide/howto_basicfeatures.xml, 'Variable Interpolation') documents only sys/const/env, so the script/url/file/dns defaults are silent and undocumented. Checked whether the lookup classes are in this repository: SCRIPT/URL/DNS/FILE are implemented in the commons-text 1.8 dependency (pom.xml 291-295), not in the snapshot, so exact per-lookup behavior (script key parsing, URL protocol handling) was not read from source here. The 'lookups are stateless and shared' javadoc in DefaultLookups is not a mitigation.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the context of the application when a script engine is present; server-side request forgery against internal/loopback services; disclosure of local file contents and environment/system properties; DNS-based data exfiltration. The weakness crosses a trust boundary whenever an application treats any configuration value as non-attacker-controlled while actually allowing user/tenant/remote influence over it, so impact is potentially confidentiality, integrity and availability of the whole JVM.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses this snapshot's default interpolator (the default for all AbstractConfiguration subclasses) and reads the attacker-influenced value through a typed getter such as getString/getInt/getLong/getBoolean/getList/getStringArray. For ${script:...} code execution a JSR-223 script engine must be available (e.g. Nashorn on Java 8-14, or any engine on the classpath); otherwise the same default set still enables ${url:...} network fetching (SSRF, including internal services and file: URIs), ${file:...}/${properties:...} local file content reads, ${dns:...} DNS exfiltration, and ${env:...}/${sys:...} information disclosure. getProperty() returns raw values and does not interpolate, so a payload must be read via a converting getter.
candidates.root_cause: ConfigurationInterpolator builds its immutable default prefix-lookup map from DefaultLookups values (SCRIPT, URL, DNS, FILE, CONST, PROPERTIES, RESOURCE_BUNDLE, XML, ...) plus Commons Text DefaultStringLookup values, and AbstractConfiguration.installDefaultInterpolator() registers that whole set on every configuration instance unconditionally. ConfigurationInterpolator.resolve() dispatches ${prefix:name} straight to the registered lookup, and DefaultConversionHandler.to() interpolates string values during typed conversion. The library therefore treats configuration values as trusted interpolation expressions and exposes script execution, arbitrary URL fetching and file reading by default, with no opt-in or filtering.
candidates.title: Default variable-interpolation lookups (script/url/dns/file) are enabled for every configuration and allow code execution, SSRF and local file disclosure from attacker-influenced configuration values
candidates.trace: Value stored in configuration (e.g. tenant property 'x = ${script:javascript:...code...}') -> AbstractConfiguration.getString("x") (line 1342) -> convert() (1778) -> getAndConvertProperty() (1748) -> getConversionHandler().to(value, cls, getInterpolator()) (1754) -> DefaultConversionHandler.to() calls interpolator.interpolate(src) (line 115) -> ConfigurationInterpolator.interpolate() (355) -> StringSubstitutor.replace() with the resolve() lambda (343) -> ConfigurationInterpolator.resolve("script:...") (485) -> fetchLookupForPrefix("script").lookup(name) (497) -> DefaultLookups.SCRIPT registered via DEFAULT_PREFIX_LOOKUPS (ConfigurationInterpolator 111-118; installDefaultInterpolator in AbstractConfiguration 452-456) -> StringLookupAdapter.lookup (StringLookupAdapter 43) -> Commons Text ScriptStringLookup evaluates the expression in a javax.script engine (dependency commons-text 1.8, pom.xml 291-295). The same dispatch exposes URL/FILE/DNS lookups registered by the identical mechanism.
candidates.unverified: No code was compiled or executed and no payload was run, so RCE/SSRF are not runtime-confirmed; the exact script-lookup key format and URL/FILE lookup protocol handling reside in Apache Commons Text 1.8 (dependency not present in the snapshot) and were inferred from the registration code and documented key list; exploitability of the script path depends on which JSR-223 engine is present on the runtime classpath.
candidates.weakness_type: Unsafe default configuration / code injection via variable interpolation (CWE-94; SSRF CWE-918; file disclosure CWE-200/538)

coverage_summary: Source scope per get_source_scope: 318 model-visible files, no binary/symlink/sensitive-path exclusions, same filters for B0/P1. Coverage included all packages under src/main/java (core config classes, interpol, convert, io, tree/xpath, builder/combined, beanutils, plist, resolver, reloading, spring, web, event, sync), pom.xml/conf/assembly, site xdoc userguide, and changes/RELEASE-NOTES. There are no test sources in the snapshot, and dependency sources (commons-text, snakeyaml, jackson, jexl, commons-lang3) are not present, so those implementations were assessed only through their usage sites.
limitations: No compilation, tests or dynamic analysis were run; all conclusions are static source reading (candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability).

The dangerous lookup implementations live in Apache Commons Text 1.8 (pom.xml dependency), which is not part of the assigned source tree; the exact script key parsing and URL/file lookup behavior could not be read here.
There is no git history or diff in the snapshot, so the change history around the identified code could not be inspected.
The snapshot contains no src/test tree, so tests that might demonstrate intended interpolation behavior could not be reviewed.

Coverage of some large classes (FileHandler, CombinedConfigurationBuilder, PropertiesConfiguration, XMLConfiguration, InMemoryNodeModel, ModelTransaction) was targeted rather than line-by-line; other latent issues there cannot be excluded.

rejected_leads.lead: YAMLConfiguration.read(Reader)/read(InputStream) use the unsafe SnakeYAML 'new Yaml()' constructor (YAMLConfiguration.java lines 68 and 120) with snakeyaml 1.25 (pom.xml 402-407); FileHandler routes file loads through InputStreamSupport.read(InputStream), so an untrusted YAML document can trigger SnakeYAML arbitrary-type instantiation.
rejected_leads.reason: Real but third-party (SnakeYAML CVE-2022-1471 family) and requires untrusted YAML to be loaded; the snapshot also exposes safe overloads read(Reader/InputStream, LoaderOptions) for callers that opt in. More dependent on external gadget classpath than the default-lookup issue, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLConfiguration.createDocumentBuilder() (lines 838-873) and XMLDocumentHelper use a plain DocumentBuilderFactory without disabling DTDs/external entities; XMLPropertiesConfiguration/XMLPropertyListConfiguration parse via SAX with resolvers that return bundled DTD streams only for known entities.
rejected_leads.reason: Potential XXE-style exposure, but JAXP default feature behavior is implementation-dependent, DefaultEntityResolver returns null for unregistered IDs (delegating to parser defaults), and configuration files are normally trusted deployment artifacts. No in-repo evidence of a concrete attacker-controlled path, so it remains an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: JNDIConfiguration performs JNDI lookups on user-supplied keys (lines 355-359, 410-414), DatabaseConfiguration concatenates table/column/configuration-name strings into SQL (lines 785-802), and PropertiesConfiguration supports file includes (lines 1845-1927).
rejected_leads.reason: These are documented, API-supplied or by-design behaviors (the caller supplies keys/table names/include paths); no new attacker-controlled injection boundary was identified beyond intended functionality.

rejected_leads.lead: ExprLookup evaluates JEXL expressions (lines 220-245) and DefaultLookups exposes CONST/PROPERTIES/RESOURCE_BUNDLE/XML lookups.
rejected_leads.reason: ExprLookup is not registered as a default prefix lookup (it must be configured explicitly via the builder), and the other lookups are part of the same root cause already reported as the single candidate rather than separate findings.

summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot of Apache Commons Configuration (pom.xml version 2.7-SNAPSHOT, 318 repository files: src/main/java, src/site, src/changes, conf and build files; no test sources present). I traced the interpolation path end-to-end and inspected the file/IO, XML, YAML/JSON, JDBC, JNDI, beanutils, tree/XPath, reloading and builder packages for attacker-controlled input reaching dangerous sinks. The single strongest candidate is the library's default interpolation lookup set: every AbstractConfiguration instance is created with ConfigurationInterpolator.getDefaultPrefixLookups(), which includes powerful Commons Text lookups (SCRIPT, URL, DNS, FILE, CONST, PROPERTIES, RESOURCE_BUNDLE, XML, etc.). Because values are interpolated on all typed getters (getString/getInt/getList/getArray/...), a value containing ${script:...}, ${url:...} or ${file:...} that is read through those getters causes the corresponding lookup to execute: JSR-223 script evaluation (RCE when an engine such as Nashorn/Java 8-14 is present), arbitrary URL/network fetch (SSRF, local file read), DNS resolution (exfiltration), or local file content disclosure. There is no allow-list, sanitization, or opt-in; the 2.7 user guide documents only sys/const/env as default prefixes, so the dangerous defaults are silent. This matches the historical default-lookup issue in this component (commonly referenced as CVE-2022-33980) but was assessed only from this snapshot's source. The finding is source-evidence based and not runtime-confirmed.
